## Quarto and GitHub Classroom

Most of the labs will be broken down into multiple tasks for you to complete. We will extensively use **GitHub Classroom** to complete the labs. We will talk about `git` and GitHub until Week 3, but for now you need to at least know how to get access to the lab files, so there are two commands you'll need to know.

Most of the code we write will be in `quarto`. Quarto is a superset of `markdown`, that allows us to write documents made purely of plain text, and **compile** or **knit** them into formatted output, such as HTML or PDF. Importantly, we can **embed `R` code** in `quarto` documents, have `quarto` run the code and embed the output of the code into the report. This is important for reproducibility; the document we write contains all the documentation needed to explain the problem, the code to produce outputs and the interpretation of the outputs, in one place.

## Palmer Penguins in `R`

We will be using the Palmer Penguins dataset, a dataset that is an alternative to the classic Iris dataset. It contains real observations of three penguin species - Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo - collected from the Palmer Station in Antarctica by researchers studying penguin ecology. The dataset includes:

- Biological measurements (e.g. flipper length, body mass, bill depth)
- Metadata (species, island, sex, year)

This dataset was curated and made accessible by Allison Horst and collaborators, and has become popular in both R and Python data science communities.

The next code block loads and processes the dataset, stored in `penguins.csv` in the repository.

::: callout-tip
If you look at the `.qmd` file in RStudio or VS Code, you will see the code appears surrounded by some backtick characters (\`). These tell `quarto` that what is contained between the backticks is code. The text after the backticks (`{r}`) tells us that this is `R` code. When `quarto` compiles this document to HTML or PDF, the code is run, and the output is placed into the document.
:::

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
head(penguins)
summary(penguins)
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Tricks for Reproducibility

The code above is **not very well written**; it doesn't explain what is happening on each line. This is bad for reproducibility. Another scientist reading your code might not understand what is happening!

To improve this we can add *comments* to the code. Comments are basically text that is ignored by the language, so that we can annotate it to explain it to other readers.

```{r}
# This is what a comment in R looks like
print("Hello world!")  # We can also add comments at the end of lines.
```

### Task 2

- [x] Add comments before each line of code in the blocks above, explaining what is happening on each line.
- [x] Add some interpretation of the plot (in `markdown`, not as comments), after the code block.
- [x] Create a second plot, below, that colours the dots by sex instead of by species.

```{r}
# Import the tidyverse package
library(tidyverse)

# Import the penguins dataset and save it as the variable penguins
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

# Display the first few rows of the penguins dataset
head(penguins)

# Display a summary of the penguins dataset
summary(penguins)

# Create a scatter plot of flipper length vs body mass, colored by species
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()

# Create a scatter plot of flipper length vs body mass, colored by sex
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()
```

The first graph shows that flipper length and body mass have a positive correlation.

If you don't know how to do something in `R` you have a few options:

- Check the documentation, e.g. by using `?ggplot` or similar.
- Use a search engine to find an answer.
- Ask a Generative AI tool. Most of them are pretty good at coding.

The next task asks you to *extend* what we have already done using new functionality of `ggplot`.

- [x] Create a third plot that uses colour for species and changes the *shape* of the points based on the sex.

```{r}
# Import the tidyverse package
library(tidyverse)

# Create a scatter plot of flipper length vs body mass, colored by species and shape depending on sex
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species, shape = sex)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Task 3

Produce plots to answer the following research questions:

- [x] On which island are we most likely to find which penguins?

```{r}
# Compare species proportions across islands
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Island",
    y = "Proportion of penguins",
    fill = "Species",
    title = "Penguin species by island"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

- [x] What is the most useful measurement or measurements to distinguish different species of penguin?

```{r}
# Reshape the measurement columns so they can be plotted in facets
penguin_measurements <- penguins |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g),
    names_to = "measurement",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Compare each measurement across penguin species
ggplot(penguin_measurements, aes(x = species, y = value, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~measurement, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Measurement value",
    fill = "Species",
    title = "Penguin measurements by species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

- [x] Do the measurements given vary significantly with the penguin's genders?

```{r}
# Compare measurements between sexes within each species
ggplot(
  filter(penguin_measurements, !is.na(sex)),
  aes(x = sex, y = value, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_grid(measurement ~ species, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Measurement value",
    fill = "Sex",
    title = "Penguin measurements by sex and species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
